issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere under Article 136 with concurrent factual findings when those findings are perverse.
material_facts: The first appellate court reversed the trial court’s dismissal of the title suit, and the High Court affirmed that reversal.

The courts below treated the defendants’ patta as invalid without properly considering evidence that it had been issued in 1929 by an authorised officer, along with revenue records and revenue-authority findings supporting the defendants’ possession.
The first appellate court inferred that the patta was issued in 1954 from a witness’s age, although the documentary evidence showed that it was issued in 1929.
issues.conclusion: The concurrent findings of the first appellate court and the High Court were perverse and could be interfered with; the Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s judgment and restored the trial court’s judgment.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, concurrent findings are not ordinarily disturbed absent compelling reasons, but the Supreme Court may interfere when the findings are perverse. The Court relied on Mahesh Dattatray Thirthkar v. State of Maharashtra (2009) 11 SCC 141.

rule.if: appeal_under_article_136 and concurrent_factual_findings and (findings_are_perverse or compelling_reasons_to_interfere)

predicates.appeal_under_article_136: A party brings an appeal to the Supreme Court under its special appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The lower appellate court and the High Court have reached the same factual conclusions.
predicates.findings_are_perverse: The lower courts’ factual conclusions disregard or misapprehend material evidence, or rest on an unsustainable inference.
predicates.compelling_reasons_to_interfere: The record presents reasons sufficiently strong to justify disturbing the concurrent findings.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges concurrent factual findings, the Supreme Court may disturb them if they are perverse or compelling reasons to interfere exist.

issues.legal_issue: An admission that a lease was originally granted does not, by itself, establish that the claimant’s title under the lease continued when the opposing pleading also asserts cancellation and a later grant to another person.
material_facts: The defendants acknowledged that the plaintiffs’ predecessors had originally received a lease for cultivation.
The defendants’ pleading also asserted that the earlier lease was cancelled after the land was abandoned and that a later auction resulted in a lease to the defendants’ predecessor.
The plaintiffs sought a declaration of title but did not produce their predecessors’ patta and relied on the admission of the original lease.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiffs could not rely selectively on the admission of the original lease; they still had to prove that their patta continued in force and that they remained its holders.
issues.legal_principle: Section 58 of the Evidence Act provides that admitted facts need not be proved, but its proviso gives the court discretion to require proof of an admitted fact. Pleadings must be read as a whole, and a claimant cannot isolate a favourable admission from the rest of the opposing pleading.

predicates.civil_title_suit: A claimant brings a civil proceeding seeking a declaration of title to property.
predicates.admission_of_original_lease: The opposing party acknowledges that the claimant’s predecessor was originally granted a lease.
predicates.pleading_also_asserts_cancellation_or_la: The opposing party’s pleading also states that the earlier lease ended or that a later grant transferred rights to someone else.

issues.definition: In a title suit, an admission of an original lease does not establish continuing title where the opposing pleading also asserts that the lease ended or the rights were later transferred.

issues.legal_issue: A court may presume the genuineness of a document that is more than thirty years old and produced from proper custody, and an unsupported allegation of fraud does not rebut that presumption.
material_facts: The defendants produced a patta issued in 1929 from their custody.
The document’s contents and endorsements referred to government-record entries made pursuant to official orders.
The plaintiffs alleged that the patta was forged but produced no evidence proving forgery.
issues.conclusion: The patta qualified for a presumption of genuineness, and the plaintiffs did not rebut that presumption.
issues.legal_principle: Section 90 of the Evidence Act permits, but does not require, a court to presume the genuineness of a document that is at least thirty years old and produced from custody the court considers proper. Mere allegations of fraud are insufficient to rebut the presumption.

rule.if: civil_evidence_issue and document_is_over_thirty_years_old and document_produced_from_proper_custody and fraud_allegation_is_unsubstantiated

predicates.civil_evidence_issue: A court must determine the evidentiary status of a document in a civil proceeding.
predicates.document_is_over_thirty_years_old: The document was made more than thirty years before it is produced in court.
predicates.document_produced_from_proper_custody: The document is produced from custody that the court considers appropriate in the circumstances.
predicates.fraud_allegation_is_unsubstantiated: A party alleges that the document is fraudulent but provides no evidence sufficient to establish that allegation.

issues.definition: For an old document produced from proper custody, an unsupported fraud allegation does not prevent the court from presuming the document genuine.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant seeking a declaration of title must establish title through the claimant’s own evidence, and revenue entries alone do not prove or confer title.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought a declaration of title and consequential possession but did not produce the patta on which they relied.
The plaintiffs relied on revenue entries in their favour for only two years, while entries for other years and the revenue-authority findings supported the defendants’ predecessor’s possession.
The evidence showed that the entries relied on by the plaintiffs had been made through misconduct, and the defendants produced a patta and evidence of continued possession.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiffs failed to establish their title, and their suit for declaration and possession was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: In a suit for declaration of title, the burden lies on the plaintiff to establish a clear title through the plaintiff’s own case; weakness in the defendant’s case cannot supply that proof. Revenue entries are maintained for revenue purposes and do not, by themselves, prove or confer title. The Court relied on Union of India v. Vasavi Co-operative Housing Society Limited (2014) 2 SCC 269.

predicates.civil_title_suit: A claimant brings a civil proceeding seeking a declaration of title to property.
predicates.claimant_lacks_sufficient_title_evidence: The claimant does not produce or otherwise prove evidence sufficient to establish the claimed title.
predicates.claimant_relies_only_on_revenue_entries: The claimant relies on revenue-record entries without other sufficient proof of title.

issues.definition: A claimant in a title suit who lacks sufficient proof of title cannot establish declaratory title by relying only on revenue entries.

issues.legal_issue: A patta granted by an authorised officer before abolition of the jagirdari system remained a valid basis for the grantee’s rights, and qualifying recorded occupants became pattedar tenants on resumption.
material_facts: The patta in favour of the defendants’ predecessor was issued in 1929, when the relevant officer had authority to grant it under the applicable revenue law.
The evidence and revenue records established the defendants’ predecessor’s grant and continued occupation of the land.

The first appellate court treated the patta as having been issued in 1954, after the relevant system had been abolished, but that date rested on an inference from a witness’s age rather than the documentary evidence.
The later land-reform law provided that a person recorded as an occupant for the required continuous period at resumption would be deemed a pattedar tenant.
issues.conclusion: The patta was validly granted in 1929, not 1954, and the lower appellate courts erred in rejecting the resulting rights on the basis that the grant was made after the grantor’s authority had ended.
issues.legal_principle: Section 44 of the Rewa State Malgujari and Kashtkari Act, 1935 authorised specified officers, including a pawaidar in the relevant circumstances, to confer pattas. Section 28 of the Vindhya Pradesh Abolition of Jagirs and Land Reforms Act, 1952 deemed a person recorded as an occupant for the specified continuous period at resumption to be a pattedar tenant. The Court also referred to Section 158(1)(d)(i) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959 concerning the later status of a qualifying pattedar tenant.

predicates.civil_land_rights_dispute: A civil proceeding concerns rights in land affected by an earlier land-tenure system and its later abolition.
predicates.patta_granted_by_authorised_officer_befo: The land grant was made by an officer authorised to make it before the relevant land resumption took effect.
predicates.occupant_recorded_for_required_period_at: The occupant was recorded as occupying the land for the continuous period required when the land was resumed.

issues.definition: Where an authorised grant preceded resumption and the occupant met the required recorded-occupancy condition, the grant remains valid and the occupant receives the resulting tenant status.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may receive additional evidence where a permitted ground under the procedural rule is met, including where the evidence has a direct and important bearing on the main issue and justice requires its admission.
material_facts: The appellants sought to introduce three revenue-authority orders in the Supreme Court.

An order already in evidence expressly referred to the Tahsildar’s 1971 order, and that order addressed whether revenue entries showing the plaintiffs’ possession had been made later and whether the entries should be corrected.
The Tahsildar’s order had a direct bearing on the main issue, while the other two proposed documents were not admitted.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court admitted the Tahsildar’s 1971 order as additional evidence but declined to admit the other two proposed documents.
issues.legal_principle: Order XLI Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits additional evidence only in specified circumstances, including where the appellate court requires it to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause. Admission is discretionary and should be used sparingly; evidence with a direct and important bearing may be admitted where the interests of justice make it imperative. The Court relied on Union of India v. Ibrahim Uddin (2012) 8 SCC 148, which discusses the rule and earlier authorities.

rule.if: appellate_proceeding and proposed_evidence_is_referred_to_in_record and evidence_has_direct_important_bearing and interests_of_justice_require_admission

predicates.appellate_proceeding: A court is deciding an appeal in which a party seeks to introduce evidence not produced below.
predicates.proposed_evidence_is_referred_to_in_reco: Evidence already properly before the appellate court refers to the proposed additional evidence.
predicates.evidence_has_direct_important_bearing: The proposed evidence directly and materially concerns the main issue in the proceeding.
predicates.interests_of_justice_require_admission: The appellate court determines that admitting the evidence is necessary in the interests of justice to address the matter fairly or pronounce judgment.

issues.definition: In an appeal, additional evidence may be admitted when the existing record refers to it, it directly and materially concerns the main issue, and justice requires its admission.
